blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: This tree follows the topics and the problem list of NeetCode's roadmap (the NeetCode 150), with a learning page written for this site for each topic. The explanations and Java templates are ours; the problems belong to LeetCode, and each one links to its LeetCode page.

Computers store integers as bits, and operating directly on those bits is both fast and, for some problems, the only way to meet a "constant extra space" requirement. The tricks are few; learning them once pays off across many problems.

| Operator | Meaning | Handy for |
|---|---|---|
| `a & b` | 1 where both are 1 | Testing a bit, clearing bits |
| `a \| b` | 1 where either is 1 | Setting a bit |
| `a ^ b` | 1 where they differ | Finding the odd one out, adding without carry |
| `~a` | Flips every bit | Masks |
| `a << k`, `a >> k` | Multiply or divide by 2ᵏ (`>>` keeps the sign) | Building masks, halving |
| `a >>> k` | Unsigned right shift (fills with zeros) | Walking all 32 bits of a negative number |

The identities worth memorising: `x ^ x = 0`, `x ^ 0 = x`, XOR is commutative and associative, `x & (x - 1)` **clears the lowest set bit**, `x & -x` **isolates the lowest set bit**, and `x & 1` is the parity.

"appears twice except one", "without extra space", "XOR", "number of 1 bits", "power of two", "subset as a mask", "add without +". A subset of up to about 20 items can be stored as one `int` mask, which is how many DP-over-subsets solutions work.
blocks.title: Signal words

blocks.text: Java `int` is **32 bits, signed, two's complement**, and `long` is 64. There are no unsigned types, so the unsigned shift `>>>` and library helpers such as `Integer.bitCount` matter.

blocks.title: BitTricks.java

blocks.text: **What to notice.** `getSum` terminates for negative numbers too, because Java `int` arithmetic wraps at 32 bits and the carry eventually shifts out. In `reverseBits`, using `>>` instead of `>>>` would work for positive inputs and quietly fail for negative ones.

- **`>>` versus `>>>`** on negative numbers. `-8 >> 1` is `-4` (sign kept); `-8 >>> 1` is a large positive number.
- **Shifting by 32 or more.** For `int`, the shift distance is taken modulo 32, so `1 << 32` equals `1`, not `0`. Use `long` (`1L << k`) when k can reach 32.
- **Operator precedence.** `==` binds tighter than `&`, so `x & 1 == 0` does not do what it looks like. Write `(x & 1) == 0`.
- **Overflow in Reverse Integer.** Check before multiplying: compare with `Integer.MAX_VALUE / 10` instead of relying on wrap-around.
- **Readability.** Say what the trick means in a comment; `n &= n - 1` is cryptic to a reader.

XOR all the numbers. A number XORed with itself is 0, and 0 XOR x is x, and XOR is order independent, so the pairs cancel and only the single number remains. If every number appears *three* times except one, count the bits at each position modulo 3 instead.
blocks.title: Interview angle: Every number in an array appears twice except one. Find it in O(1) space.
Key points
blocks.text:
- `x & (x - 1)` clears the lowest set bit; `x & -x` isolates it
- `x ^ x = 0` and `x ^ 0 = x` make XOR the tool for "find the odd one out"
- Java `int` is 32-bit signed: use `>>>` to shift without the sign and `1L << k` for k >= 32
- XOR is addition without carry; AND shifted left is the carry
- Parenthesise bit tests: `(x & 1) == 0`
- A small set can be a bitmask in an `int`

blocks.title: Practise and track them
blocks.text: Open **Practice** in the top bar and choose **Bit Manipulation** (under DSA by topic) to tick problems off, keep notes on each one, and add problems of your own.

items.question: What does `n & (n - 1)` do and how does it count set bits?
items.answer: It clears the lowest set bit of n. Repeating it until n is zero takes one iteration per set bit, so the loop count is the number of 1 bits.

items.question: Why do you use `>>>` instead of `>>` when reversing bits?
items.answer: `>>` copies the sign bit into the vacated positions, so for a negative number the loop would shift in ones and never reach zero in the intended way. `>>>` always shifts in zeros, so all 32 bits are processed correctly.

items.question: How can you add two integers without using `+`?
items.answer: XOR gives the sum of each bit without carry and `(a & b) << 1` gives the carries. Replace `a` with the XOR and `b` with the carries and repeat until there are no carries left.
